lesson.title: Roads, Canals, and Rails: The Infrastructure Behind a National Market
lesson.summary: A wave of road, canal, and railroad construction in the early nineteenth century collapsed the time and cost of moving goods and people, providing the physical backbone that made the Market Revolution's national economy possible.
lesson.body:
The Market Revolution needed a way to actually move goods across long distances cheaply, and for most of the early republic that was the young nation's biggest economic obstacle. Roads were often unpaved and nearly impassable in bad weather, and shipping heavy goods overland any real distance cost far more than the goods themselves were worth. The federal government made an early attempt to address this with the National Road, sometimes called the Cumberland Road, begun in 1811 and eventually stretching from Cumberland, Maryland toward the Ohio Valley, the first major federally funded interstate highway in American history.

Water transportation offered a cheaper alternative, and two innovations transformed it almost simultaneously. Robert Fulton demonstrated the commercial potential of the steamboat in 1807 when his vessel, popularly remembered as the Clermont, successfully traveled up New York's Hudson River under steam power, proving that boats no longer needed to depend on favorable wind or the slow labor of poling and rowing against a current. Steamboats soon spread to the Mississippi, Ohio, and other interior rivers, making upstream travel practical for the first time and dramatically cutting the cost of shipping farm goods to market.

Canals delivered an even bigger leap. New York State, under the political leadership of Governor DeWitt Clinton, financed and built the Erie Canal between 1817 and 1825, a 363 mile artificial waterway connecting the Hudson River at Albany to Lake Erie at Buffalo. The canal cut the cost of shipping goods between the Great Lakes region and New York City by a huge margin and slashed travel time to match, and its success touched off a nationwide canal building boom as other states rushed to build their own connections to the expanding national market described in the Market Revolution.

Railroads arrived soon after and would eventually surpass both roads and canals combined. The Baltimore and Ohio Railroad received its charter in 1827 and began carrying passengers and freight in 1830, among the first common carrier railroads in the United States, using steam locomotives to pull cars along fixed iron rails regardless of weather, season, or the presence of a navigable river. Rail construction remained modest through the 1830s compared to what would follow in the 1850s, but the technology's advantages over water transportation, speed, flexibility of route, and the ability to reach places with no river or lake nearby, were already obvious to investors and farmers alike.

Together these networks of road, canal, and rail did more than move cargo faster. They physically stitched together a country whose regions had specialized so sharply under the Market Revolution, letting a farmer in Ohio sell wheat in New York and letting a Massachusetts mill sell cloth in the Mississippi Valley, and in doing so they turned the abstract idea of a single American economy into a lived, everyday reality that would keep accelerating for the rest of the century.
